name: The Founder Effect
statement: A population started by a few carries only a chance sliver of the original's genes.
meaning: The founder effect is the loss of genetic variation that occurs when a new population is established by a small number of individuals drawn from a larger one. Because the founders carry only a small, non-random sample of the source population's genes, the new population has reduced diversity and allele frequencies that differ from the source by chance — some alleles lost entirely, others over-represented. It is a sampling phenomenon, not an adaptive one.
mechanism: The founding group is a small random draw from the parent gene pool, so its allele frequencies deviate from the source purely by sampling error, and the smaller the group the larger the expected deviation. In the small new population, drift then continues to swing frequencies from generation to generation, while matings between relatives grow more likely, raising homozygosity and exposing recessive alleles. A rare allele in the source can become common in the offshoot, or vanish, with no help from selection. It is a special case of genetic drift, close kin to the bottleneck effect.

examples.text: A high frequency of variegate porphyria among Afrikaners traces to a single seventeenth-century Dutch settler couple, the disease allele carried in by a few founders and amplified by isolation.

Ellis-van Creveld syndrome runs high among the Old Order Amish, and on the atoll of Pingelap complete colourblindness affects about a tenth of the population, traced to a 1775 typhoon that left around twenty survivors, one a carrier.
A founder bottleneck and long isolation left Finns with dozens of otherwise rare recessive disorders enriched in the population — a whole heritage of founder-effect diseases.

variants.name: The bottleneck effect
variants.text: The related case in which an existing population is drastically reduced by a disaster and the survivors' gene pool is a small sample of the former one, as in the northern elephant seal.

variants.name: Founder-effect speciation
variants.text: Mayr's stronger claim that founder events trigger genetic revolutions that drive speciation — a contested idea now less favoured after Barton and Charlesworth's critique.

whyItMatters: It explains why isolated and newly founded populations, from island colonists to human diaspora communities, so often show reduced diversity and elevated rates of rare recessive diseases. It is central to conservation genetics, where small founding numbers threaten the genetic health of reintroduced populations, and to understanding how populations diverge.

working.text: treat a population founded by few individuals as carrying only a fraction of the source's variation, with shifted allele frequencies.
anticipate elevated frequencies of otherwise rare recessive diseases in isolated founder populations, from inbreeding and amplified founder alleles.
in conservation, use enough genetically diverse founders to avoid baking in an impoverished gene pool.

limits: The general genetic founder effect — reduced diversity and shifted frequencies in an offshoot — is well established and robust. But Mayr's stronger claim, that founder events trigger genetic revolutions that cause speciation, is contested and now less favoured, Barton and Charlesworth having argued it is a low-probability process with thin theoretical justification and equivocal laboratory support. And not every high-frequency disease in an isolated group is pure founder effect: in some cases, such as Tay-Sachs among Ashkenazi Jews, balancing selection through heterozygote advantage may also contribute, and the attribution is genuinely debated.
misreadings: The founder effect is not a form of natural selection but genetic drift — the shifts in allele frequency are driven by chance sampling, not fitness, which is why a harmful recessive can rise precisely because selection is not driving it. It is not the same as the bottleneck effect, which reduces an existing population rather than founding a new one. And founder events do not routinely create new species; that stronger claim is the contested part.
origin: Introduced by Ernst Mayr, who first outlined it in 'Systematics and the Origin of Species' (1942) and developed the founder principle and his genetic-revolution model in 1954; it is understood as a special case of the genetic drift theorised by Sewall Wright.

sources.text: Founder effect, Wikipedia. — the small-sample definition, the disease examples, the tie to genetic drift, and the bottleneck distinction.
Barton & Charlesworth, "Genetic Revolutions, Founder Effects, and Speciation," Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 15:133-164 (1984). — the critique of founder-effect speciation.
The Finnish genetic heritage in 2022, Disease Models & Mechanisms 15(10). — the founder bottleneck behind the Finnish disease heritage.
